title: Eggs are prolate spheroids, never oblate

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Eggs are prolate spheroids, never oblate

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Hard-shelled eggs, while often pointed, are never flattened or discoidal: they are prolate, never oblate, solids of revolution.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: It is an obvious but by no means negligible fact that the egg, while often pointed, is never flattened or discoidal; it is a prolate, but never an oblate, spheroid.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XV, “On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures”; topic “Shapes of birds' eggs”. Scope: eggs of birds, tortoises and crocodiles

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch15-01: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.92

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Shape class is directly measurable, and the universal assertion is vulnerable to clear counterexamples. Extensive public museum imagery makes a broad and decisive test feasible.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compute principal-axis ratios and rotational asymmetry from large image or 3D samples of bird, tortoise and crocodile eggs, classifying prolate, oblate and non-axisymmetric forms with preset thresholds. Any credible oblate or discoidal hard-shelled egg refutes the absolute claim; consistently prolate samples support it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Museum egg collections have taxonomic and collecting biases.

Two-dimensional images can misclassify non-axisymmetric eggs.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.92
data existence: 0.9
discriminating power: 0.98
operationalizability: 0.99

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Prolate versus oblate is read directly from length and breadth, and two large open bird-egg compilations already contain those measurements. An oblate bird egg would be visible immediately, so the claim is decidable for the animals that dominate the chapter. Reptile eggs remain outside the files, which limits the stated scope without preventing a clear test for birds.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Classify each egg by whether length exceeds width (prolate or spherical) or width exceeds length (oblate), using species-level shape measurements. The claim is confirmed if oblate eggs are absent across the measured hard-shelled eggs; a single well-measured oblate species would refute the universal negative.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Spherical eggs sit on the boundary and need a measurement-error rule before being called prolate.

Both open compilations are birds; tortoise and crocodile eggs are a stated part of the scope and are not in these files.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: In species-level egg measurements of birds, turtles/tortoises and crocodilians, the polar axis (egg length) is never shorter than the maximum equatorial diameter (egg breadth): no hard-shelled egg is oblate or discoidal.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Downloaded the Amniote Life-History Database CSV (21,322 rows), kept rows with both egg_length_mm and egg_width_mm recorded (594 species), and computed elongation L/B per species. Species were grouped as Aves (167), Testudines (16), Crocodilia (9) in scope and Squamata (402) out of scope. For each group the count of species with L/B < 1.00 (oblate as recorded), L/B < 0.98 (robustly oblate) and L/B < 1.05 (near-spherical) was tabulated with the minimum and quantiles of L/B.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. For each species with a mean egg length L (pole-to-pole) and breadth B (maximum equatorial diameter) in the Deeming & Ruta 2014 amniote egg compilation (Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.s9227) and the 955-species bird egg-shape compilation (Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.sj3tx9648), compute the elongation L/B. Groups: birds, Testudines, Crocodylia (hard-shelled, in scope); Squamata reported separately as out of scope (mostly parchment-shelled). Supports if, in every in-scope group, zero species have L/B < 1.00, and the fraction of species within 5% of a sphere (L/B < 1.05) is reported together with the minimum L/B per group.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Refutes if any in-scope species has a mean L/B < 0.98 (polar axis robustly shorter than equatorial diameter, beyond ~2% measurement error) in either compilation. Mixed if the smallest in-scope L/B lies in [0.98, 1.00), i.e. a species indistinguishable from oblate within measurement error.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: minimum species-mean egg length/breadth among in-scope species (Macrochelys temminckii, 38.8 x 37.5 mm); zero of 192 species have L/B < 1

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: no oblate species found; in-scope L/B 1st-99th percentile 1.15-1.90

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Thompson's 'prolate, never oblate spheroid' is read as: the axis of rotational symmetry (the pole-to-pole length, which in asymmetric eggs runs through the blunt and pointed ends) exceeds the equatorial diameter. Published egg measurements record length and breadth with length along the polar axis, so L/B >= 1 means prolate and L/B < 1 would mean oblate. A limitation stated up front: because measurers conventionally record the longer dimension as length, a truly oblate egg could only reveal itself in such data as L/B at or just below 1 (an apparently spherical egg); the test therefore asks whether any species approaches that boundary, and the fraction of near-spherical eggs is reported as the zone where the data cannot discriminate.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Amniote Life-History Database (Myhrvold et al. 2015, Ecology 96:3109; Ecological Archives E096-269)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Deviation from pre-registration: the two Dryad compilations named in planned_datasets (doi:10.5061/dryad.s9227, doi:10.5061/dryad.sj3tx9648) could not be downloaded because Dryad's file downloads are gated by an interactive anti-bot (proof-of-work) challenge; the Amniote Life-History Database, which carries the same two variables (egg length, egg width) and also covers turtles and crocodilians, was substituted. Criteria and thresholds were not changed.

Coverage is modest: only 167 bird, 16 turtle and 9 crocodilian species have both egg length and width in this database, far fewer than the ~1,400 bird species of Stoddard et al. 2017. A rare oblate species could be missed; a universal negative can only be supported, not proven, by a sample.

Measurement convention limits discriminating power: because egg length is recorded along the longer (polar) axis, an oblate egg could only appear as L/B at or just below 1. The data show no species near that boundary except the alligator snapping turtle (L/B = 1.03, effectively spherical), so the data are consistent with the claim but cannot exclude an oblate egg disguised as a sphere.

One crocodilian row (L/B = 16.9) is an evident unit error in the source (width probably in cm); it does not affect the oblate count and is left as recorded.

Squamata (402 species, mostly parchment-shelled, min L/B = 1.00 in a gecko) are outside Thompson's 'hard-shelled' scope and are reported only for completeness.
